senses.gloss:
buddhi
(‘that by which [an object] is known’, the intellect)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘buddhi,’ indicating the intellect, is sometimes used as a general term for the मिन्द्. At other times it is applied to the discriminative faculty of the मिन्द्. According to the Advaita Vedānta, the जीव (individual सोउल्) is the reflection of the आत्मन् in this बुद्धि.
See ANTAḤKARAṆA for details.

Buddhiyoga
(‘the योग of बुद्धि or intellect’)
------------------------------------------
This is a unique word used only in the Bhagavadgītā and that too, only three times (2.49; 10.10 and 18.57).
‘Buddhi’ means the intellect and ‘yoga’ means perfect concentration as well as union. So, the path of spiritual discipline wherein the बुद्धि plays an important role and ultimately leads to the union of the जीव (the individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् (God) is बुद्धियोग.
Karma or action normally binds a person due to the selfish desires behind it. If कर्म is performed with the full understanding that its motivation by selfish desires leads to सṁसार or the bondage of transmigration, and that, if motivated by the spirit of unselfish service and devotion to God, the same will lead to लिबेरतिओन्, it becomes बुद्धियोग since this leads to the ultimate union with God.
The commentators of the Bhagavad-gītā have interpreted it variously, depending upon the context. However, all the interpretations boil down to the same meaning as given above.
These are some of them: कर्म per-formed with equanimity; niṣkāma-कर्म-योग that leads to आत्मज्ञान or self-know-ledge; योग endowed with the vision of the आत्मन्; uniting the मिन्द् with God and so on.
See also BHAGAVADGĪTĀ.

Buddha
(‘The Enlightened One’)
------------------------------------------
Buddha (also known as गौतम बुद्ध and Śākya मुनि) is one of the very few religious leaders of the world who have revolutionised the life of a very large mass of people for generations, influencing their religion, philosophy and culture including many aspects of arts and sciences.
Born on a Vaiśākha pūrṇimā day, as the only son of Śuddhodana (the king of Kapilavāstu) and Māyādevī (at Lumbiṇī, now in Nepal), he was named Siddhārtha. He lived an easy and protected life as the beloved prince and heir to the throne up to the age of 29 years. He was married to the princess Yaśodharā and had a son (Rāhula) by her. One day (for the first time in his life), he went out to see the city. The sight of an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a monk made a deep impression on his मिन्द्. He then realized that life was full of suffering and decided to become a monk to discover the path to blessedness, totally free of all suffering. He renounced the world on a Vaiśākha pūrṇimā day, retired to a forest and practised very severe austerities but to no avail. He then sat under a tree on the bank of the river Nairāñjanā in गया vowing that he would not get up from his seat until he realized the truth. Soon, he was enlightened and it was again on a Vaiśākha pūrṇimā day. The tree came to be known as ‘Bodhivṛkṣa’ and he became the बुद्ध, the enlightened one. He then went to वाराणसी (Kāśī) and gave his first sermon there. This sermon came to be known as dharmacakrapravartana or the discourse of setting in motion, the wheel of धर्म. He was 35 at that time. He lived up to 80. For a long period of 45 years he roamed about the country teaching his doctrines of spiritual wisdom to one and all. He established a Saṅgha or a religious order of his monastic disciples to propagate his teachings. He passed away, again, on a Vaiśākha pūrṇimā day. Hence this day is called the thrice-blessed day.
As regards the period of बुद्ध’s life the dates vary from 624 B.C.-544 B.C. up to 557 B.C.-477 B.C. It may be safely assumed that he lived during the sixth century B.C.
Buddha’s teachings may be summarized as follows:
Buddha teaches ‘catvāri āryasatyāni,’ the four noble truths. They are:
duḥkha or the existence of suffering in this world;
duḥkha-samudāya or that there is a cause for this suffering;
duḥkhanirodha or that it is possible to stop this suffering;
duḥkha-nirodha-mārga or that there is a way out of this suffering.
He calls the last as the ārya-aṣṭāṅgika-mārga, or the eightfold noble path. These eight steps are: samyag-dṛṣṭi (right views), samyak-सङ्कल्प (right resolve), samyag-vāk (right speech), samyak-karmānta (right conduct), samyag-ājīva (right livelihood), samyag-vyāyāma (right effort), samyak-स्मृति (right mindfulness) and samyak-समाधि (right concentration).
Buddha calls the state of enlightenment as निर्वाण which, literally, means extinction (of all sorrow and suffering).
Compilation, preservation and elaboration of बुद्ध’s teachings (leading to several schools of बुद्धिस्म् and Buddhist philosophy) took place over centuries through several Buddhist Councils. The Vinaya Piṭaka and the Sutta Piṭaka containing the rules for guiding the मोन्क्स् and the direct teachings of बुद्ध were compiled during the first Buddhist Council held immediately after बुद्ध’s demise. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka was compiled during the third Council conducted by the emperor अशोक (3rd century B.C.). The work is abstruse and philosophical and contains the teachings of बुद्ध’s disciples and scholars of the tradition.
The three works together are known as the Tripiṭaka or the Tipiṭaka and are the canonical works of बुद्धिस्म्.
See also BUDDHISM.

Buddhism
(‘religious principles and doctrines taught by बुद्ध’)
------------------------------------------
‘Buddhism’ is the general name given by post-बुद्ध historians to the religious principles and practices, doctrines and dogmas, of the followers of गौतम बुद्ध. Though what बुद्ध taught might be regarded as a cleansing or reformation of the हिन्दुइस्म् of his times, his teachings, over the centuries, have attained a distinctive character of their own, thus deserving the appellation ‘Buddhism’ or ‘Buddha-mata’ or ‘Bauddha-धर्म’.
The four noble truths (catvāri āryasatyāni) and the eightfold noble path (ārya-aṣṭāṅgika-mārga) form the core of बुद्धिस्म्. अहिṁसा or non-injury or non-violence is a cardinal ethical principle. Monastic life, as means to निर्वाण (libe-ration) and बुद्ध-hood is emphasized greatly.
During the second Buddhist Council held at Vaiśāli (the present Basarh of Bihar) about a 100 years after the demise of बुद्ध, there was a split in the ranks of the Buddhists. The conservatives came to be known as the Sthaviravādis or Theravādis. The rest came to be called the Mahāsāṅghikas. These two groups gradually evolved the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna schools. The former stressed individual निर्वाण as the goal of life. The latter stressed compassion, in addition, so that all can be helped in their attempts at obtaining निर्वाण. Whereas Mahāyāna flourished in China, Japan and Tibet, Hīnayāna spread in Śrī लङ्का, Myanmar (Burma) and some South East Asian countries.
Buddhism also developed in course of time, four schools of philosophy: the Mādhyamika or Śūnyavāda, the Yogācāra or Vijñānavāda, the Sautrāntika and the Vaibhāṣika.
Philosophical works on these schools were written both in Pāḷī and Sanskrit languages.
See also BUDDHA.
